title: Why one low tide is lower
teaches: The Moon's tilt, the tide as a sum of regular waves, Kelvin's tide-predicting machine, and why summer's lowest tides come in daylight
summary: **Seattle's two daily tides are unequal.** Most days have a lower low and a higher low, often several feet apart, and the two highs differ too.

**The Moon's tilt makes the difference.** The Moon swings up to about 28° north and south of the equator each month, which tilts the two bulges so that Seattle passes through a thick part of one and a thin part of the other.
**The difference comes and goes every two weeks.** It is biggest when the Moon is furthest north or south and almost gone when the Moon crosses the equator, a cycle separate from springs and neaps.
**Two steady waves of nearly equal period add to an uneven pattern.** They drift in and out of step, so the sum swells and shrinks over days.
**The tide is a sum of constituents.** Each is a steady wave with its own period: M2 (12.42 h) and S2 (12 h) twice a day, K1 (23.93 h) and O1 (25.82 h) once a day.
**The daily waves are what split the lows.** At Seattle K1 and O1 together are about as big as M2 and S2, which makes its tide mixed.

**Kelvin measured the tide instead of solving it.** Laplace's equations could not be solved for real seas, so Kelvin took each constituent's size and timing from a port's gauge records and built a machine in 1872 that added them.
**Tide tables are still made this way.** Machines did it with pulleys and a wire until the 1960s; computers now add the same waves.

**Summer's lowest lows come in daylight at Seattle.** The Sun's tilt adds a daily wave that keeps to the clock, and it flips by twelve hours between June and December, so winter's lowest lows come at night.

blocks.text: In late May 1792 [[George Vancouver]]'s two ships lay at anchor in the Sound while their boats explored it. Lieutenant [[Peter Puget]] took two boats south for a week, past the Narrows and into the inlets beyond, rowing by day and camping on the beaches at night. Anyone who lives on a beach like that, hauling boats up and down it twice a day, meets the habit of this sea quickly: of the two low tides each day, one goes out much further than the other, and the difference grows and shrinks from one week to the next. The two equal bulges of lesson 8, taken alone, would give two equal tides a day.

The tide table for Seattle shows it plainly. A mid-June day can run like this: a high of about 11 feet in the early morning, a low of minus 3 feet at lunchtime, a high of 12 feet in the evening, and then a low that only gets down to 7 feet, a little after midnight. The two lows of that day are 10 feet apart. On other days the lows are nearly equal and the highs differ instead, and on a few days a month everything is close to even.

Lesson 8 built the two bulges: the Moon pulls the near side of the Earth a little harder than the centre, and the centre a little harder than the far side, so the ocean stretches into a bulge facing the Moon and another facing away. The Earth turns under both, which gives two high tides and two low tides each day. If the bulges were the same size and the Earth turned evenly under them, every place would see two equal tides. Something about the Moon must make Seattle's two passes under the bulges different. It is worth thinking about what that could be before reading on.

The Moon does not stay over the equator. Its path around the Earth is tilted, so over each month of about 27 days it swings north of the equator, crosses back, swings south and returns. At its furthest the Moon stands about 28° north or south of the equator in these years, which is called its **declination**.[^standstill] The two bulges point toward the Moon and away from it, so when the Moon is far north the near bulge is tilted up into the northern hemisphere and the far bulge down into the southern.

Now follow Seattle as the Earth turns. Seattle sits at about 47.6° north and goes round on its circle of latitude once a day. With the bulge tilted, that circle cuts through the thick middle of the near bulge on one side of the Earth and only skims the thin edge of the far bulge on the other. One high water is deep and the other shallow. Newton saw this effect of the tilt in 1687, in the same book as the bulges.

blocks.caption: The Earth seen side on, with the Moon to the right and the water's two bulges drawn far thicker than life. Seattle's dot goes round its line of latitude once a day (filled while it is on the side of the Earth facing you). Below, the water over Seattle through one turn, in Newton's picture.
blocks.task: Tilt the Moon at least 20° north or south and play a day

blocks.text: Twice a month the Moon crosses the equator. Then the bulges are not tilted, Seattle passes through both at the same depth, and the two tides of the day are nearly equal. A week later the Moon is at its furthest north or south and the difference is greatest. So the inequality comes and goes on a cycle of about two weeks, set by the Moon's swing north and south. It is a different clock from lesson 8's springs and neaps, which follow the Moon's phase, and the two drift past each other through the year.

Newton's picture puts the difference in the high waters. In the Sound it falls mostly on the lows, with a smaller difference in the highs. The bulges are a forcing, not the tide itself: the real ocean answers with waves that take hours to cross it and reach Seattle at their own times, and the daily part of the answer arrives on a different schedule from the twice-daily part. To see how that moves the difference from the highs to the lows, the tide has to be pulled apart into its pieces.

Start with two plain waves, each rising and falling at its own steady rate. Add them together, hour by hour. If they have exactly the same period they stay in step and the sum is a single bigger wave. If one is slightly slower, it drops a little further behind on every cycle, so for a while the two crests coincide and the sum swings widely, then the crests fall opposite the troughs and the sum is small, and then they come back into step.

blocks.caption: Top: two steady waves over three days, one every 12 hours and one whose period you set. Bottom: their sum over a month.

blocks.text: Nothing in either wave changes, yet their sum looks irregular, with big swings, small swings and everything between. The closer the two periods, the longer they take to drift apart and back, and at 12 hours and 12.42 hours the sum swells and shrinks every 14.8 days. Those are the Sun's and the Moon's twice-daily waves, and the pattern is the spring and neap cycle from lesson 8, seen as two steady waves adding.

The same trick works the other way round: any tide that repeats its patterns, however tangled it looks, can be pulled apart into steady waves, each with a period fixed by some cycle of the Moon or the Sun. Each of these waves is called a **constituent**. Four carry most of the tide at Seattle:[^names]

blocks.title: Seattle's four main constituents (about)
points: [[M2|moon]]: the Moon's twice-daily wave, every 12.42 hours, about 1.07 m (3.5 ft) high.
[[S2|sun]]: the Sun's twice-daily wave, every 12 hours, about 0.26 m (0.9 ft).
[[K1|moon]]: a daily wave every 23.93 hours, from the tilt of both Moon and Sun, about 0.83 m (2.7 ft).
[[O1|moon]]: a daily wave every 25.82 hours, from the Moon's tilt, about 0.46 m (1.5 ft).

blocks.text: K1 and O1 are the tilt from the last part, written as steady waves. The tilt makes a once-a-day rise and fall that is strong while the Moon is far north or south and fades as it crosses the equator. A daily wave that swells and fades every two weeks is exactly what two steady daily waves of slightly different period make when they add, as the figure above showed for the twice-daily pair. K1 and O1 fall in and out of step every 13.66 days, half the Moon's month from north to south and back.[^pair]

Lay a once-a-day wave on top of a twice-a-day wave and one of the two daily lows lands where the daily wave is also low, so it goes deeper; the other lands where the daily wave is high, so it is held up. Whether the split shows in the lows or the highs depends on when the daily wave peaks compared with the twice-daily one, and at Seattle that timing puts most of it in the lows.

blocks.caption: A model of the tide over two weeks of May, made from four constituents. M2 and S2 start at Seattle's sizes; K1 and O1 start at zero, as if the Moon and Sun never left the equator. Dots mark the lows. Seattle sets all four to Seattle's values.
blocks.task: Raise K1 and O1 (or lower M2 and S2) until some day has only one low

blocks.text: One number sums up the balance: the **form number**, K1 plus O1 divided by M2 plus S2. Under about a quarter, the daily waves hardly show and a place has two nearly equal tides a day, as most of the Atlantic coast of North America does. Over about three, the daily waves win and most days have one high and one low, as along parts of the Gulf of Mexico. Seattle's form number is close to one, a **mixed** tide: two tides a day, strongly unequal, with the lower low the one beach walkers wait for.

Knowing the periods is not enough to predict a tide. A constituent's size and timing at a port depend on how the oceans, the Strait and the Sound answer the pull, and that is a question about water moving in real basins. In 1775 and 1776 the French mathematician [[Pierre-Simon Laplace]] wrote down the equations for it: the ocean as a thin layer on a spinning Earth, set moving by the Moon and Sun, its tide a wave rather than a bulge standing still. They were right, and nobody could solve them for oceans with real coasts and depths.[^laplace]

The way round came from Glasgow. From 1867 [[William Thomson]], later Lord Kelvin, led a committee of the British Association that gave up on deriving each port's tide from first principles and measured it instead. Take a long record of hourly heights from a tide gauge, a year if possible. For each known period, find the size and timing of the steady wave hidden in the record: this is **harmonic analysis**. Then to predict the tide for any day in the future, add those waves back together. The arithmetic was the problem, since a year of predictions for one port meant thousands of sums of a dozen cosines.

So in 1872 Kelvin designed a machine to do the adding. Each constituent got a crank that turns once per period, set to its port's timing, and a pulley that the crank lifts and lowers by the right amount. A single wire runs over all the pulleys, fixed at one end, with a pen on the other. Every pulley that rises takes up a little wire and every one that falls lets some out, so the pen moves by the sum of all of them and draws the tide on a roll of paper as the handle turns.

blocks.caption: A tide-predicting machine with Seattle's four main constituents. Each crank turns at its own constituent's rate, the wire over the pulleys adds their movements, and the pen draws the sum. Kelvin's first machine had ten cranks.
blocks.task: Turn the handle through two days

blocks.text: The first machine, built in 1872 and 1873, could draw a year of tides for a port in a few hours. Others followed in several countries. The US Coast and Geodetic Survey's Tide Predicting Machine No. 2, a brass machine that added 37 constituents, made the country's tide tables, Seattle's among them, from about 1912 until the mid-1960s, when electronic computers took over the same sums.[^brass]

blocks.caption: From Newton's bulges to the tide tables.

events.label: US Machine No. 2 makes the tables

blocks.text: Today's Seattle tide table is still a sum of steady waves, each measured from the gauge on the Seattle waterfront. What the sum cannot include is weather: a deep low or a strong south wind can lift the water a foot or more above the prediction, which lesson 10 picks up.

The tide tables count heights from a zero called **mean lower low water**: the average, over many years, of the lower of each day's two lows.[^datum] A low below that zero is a **minus tide**, and the lowest of them uncover sea stars, moon snails and eelgrass that are under water most of the year. Seattle's naturalists plan their summer around them, and in June and July the best come in the middle of the day. In December and January the same deep lows come in the middle of the night.

The Moon's tilt cannot explain that, because the Moon keeps no regular clock time: its tides come about 50 minutes later each day. Something tied to the Sun must be at work. The Sun's path is tilted too, north of the equator in June and south in December, and its tilt makes a once-a-day wave of its own, carried by K1 and a smaller constituent called P1. Unlike the Moon's, this wave keeps to the clock, rising and falling at the same time of day for weeks on end. When the Sun crosses to the other side of the equator the wave turns over, so its low moves by twelve hours. At Seattle, in the months around June, it lands near midday, deepening whichever lunar low falls then; around December it lands near midnight.

blocks.caption: A model year at Seattle, from five constituents (M2, S2, K1, O1, P1): each dot is a day's lowest low, at its time of day. The bigger blue dots are minus tides. They gather around noon from spring to late summer and around midnight in winter. Times are sun time: noon is when the Sun is highest, a little after 1 pm on a Seattle summer clock.

blocks.text: Each month the minus tides arrive in a run of a few days, when a spring tide and the Moon's far swing north or south come together, and on each day of the run the low comes about 40 to 50 minutes later than the day before. That is enough to plan a low-tide walk from the table alone.

blocks.title: Outdoors: a minus tide
points: Look up the Seattle station on NOAA's tide predictions for May, June or July, and find a run of days with a low of minus 2 feet or lower in daylight.
Go to Constellation Park in West Seattle, Lincoln Park or the North Beach at Discovery Park an hour before the predicted low.
Mark the water's edge with a stick every ten minutes. Note when the water stops falling, and how far the beach runs out compared with an ordinary afternoon's low.

blocks.caption: Six questions on unequal tides
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why are the two low tides of a day at Seattle often very different in depth?
choices: The Moon's tilt north or south of the equator tilts the bulges, so Seattle passes through a thick part of one and a thin part of the other
The Sun pulls the water one way in the morning and the Moon pulls it the other way in the afternoon
The wind blows harder by day than by night, piling water against the shore in the afternoon
items.why: With the Moon far north or south, the bulges are tilted. Seattle's circle of latitude cuts deep through one and only skims the other, so the two tides of the day differ.

items.ask: The Moon is crossing the equator this week. What does that do to the difference between Seattle's two daily tides?
choices: It makes the difference smallest, because the bulges are not tilted
It makes the difference greatest, because the Moon is closest to the Earth
It has no effect; the difference follows the Moon's phase, new and full
items.why: With the Moon over the equator, Seattle passes through both bulges at the same depth. The difference is greatest about a week later, when the Moon is furthest north or south.

choices: One steady wave with a fixed period set by a cycle of the Moon or Sun; the tide is the sum of many
The part of the tide caused by one basin, such as the Strait or the Sound
The average height of high water at a port over a nineteen-year record
items.why: M2, S2, K1, O1 and the rest are each a steady rise and fall at one period. Added together, they make a tide that looks irregular but can be predicted.

items.ask: Why did Kelvin's method predict tides when Laplace's equations could not?
choices: It measured each constituent's size and timing at a port from gauge records, so nobody had to solve how the ocean answers the pull
Kelvin's machine solved Laplace's equations mechanically, one ocean basin at a time
Kelvin found that Laplace had made an error, and corrected equations could be solved by hand
items.why: Harmonic analysis takes each wave's size and timing from the port's own record, which already contains the ocean's response. Predicting is then only a matter of adding the waves, which the machine did.

items.ask: At one port K1 plus O1 is three times M2 plus S2. What tide do people there see on most days?
choices: One high and one low a day
Two nearly equal highs and lows a day
Four highs and lows a day, two large and two small
items.why: With the daily constituents that strong, the second low of most days climbs up into the high and disappears. A form number above about three means a once-a-day tide.

items.ask: Why do Seattle's lowest summer tides come in daylight while winter's come at night?
choices: The Sun's tilt adds a daily wave that keeps to the clock, and it turns over between June and December
Long summer days warm and expand the water, lowering it in the afternoon
Winter storms hold the water up during the day, so only night lows can go deep
items.why: The Moon's tides come about 50 minutes later each day, but the Sun's daily wave keeps clock time. With the Sun north in June its low falls near midday at Seattle; with the Sun south in December the same wave is turned over and its low falls near midnight.

standstill.title: How far the Moon swings
standstill.text: The Moon's furthest swing north and south changes over an 18.6-year cycle, from about 18° to about 28.5°. It was at its widest around 2024 and 2025, and will be at its narrowest in the early 2030s. Wider swings mean bigger differences between the two daily tides.

names.title: Why the odd names
names.text: The labels come from the nineteenth-century tables of harmonic analysis: M for the Moon, S for the Sun (*sol*), while K and O are only letters. The number counts crests a day, 2 for twice-daily waves and 1 for daily ones. NOAA uses 37 constituents for Seattle's predictions; the four here carry most of the range.

pair.title: One swelling wave, or two steady ones
pair.text: A wave of period 24.84 hours (the Moon's day) whose size rises and falls every 13.66 days is the same, by a rule of trigonometry, as two steady waves with periods of 23.93 and 25.82 hours added together. Tide tables use the steady pair because steady waves are easy to measure and to add.

laplace.title: Laplace's equations today
laplace.text: Laplace could solve his equations only for an idealised ocean covering the whole globe at an even depth. Computers now solve them for the real oceans, and since the 1990s satellites that measure the height of the sea surface have checked the results against the open-ocean tide measured from space. Harbour tide tables still come from harmonic analysis of each port's own gauge.

brass.title: Old Brass Brains
brass.text: Machine No. 2 was nicknamed Old Brass Brains. It was designed at the Coast and Geodetic Survey by Rollin Harris and E. G. Fischer. NOAA still keeps it.

datum.title: The zero of a tide table
datum.text: Mean lower low water is averaged over a 19-year period, the National Tidal Datum Epoch, long enough to take in the Moon's 18.6-year cycle. Charts give depths below the same zero, so a sailor adds the tide table's height to the charted depth to get the water under the keel.
